doc.title: Barry Kernfeld interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 16, 2020

title: The Real Book and Steve Swallow's story of royalties
summary: The Real Book composers found that recordings of their tunes earned far more than sheet music would have.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Okay. It’s sort of an oxymoron because all this delivery, the methods keep improving and at the same time they’re trying to put restrictions on what you can do with it and so forth.

Well it was very interesting about The Real Book and this is a good example of the ways in which say 1973 or ’75, whenever it was, was no longer 1909, the way the world had changed. There was a huge resistance to fake books, to publishing bootleg copies of notated jazz songs because that infringed upon the publishing rights, the royalties that went 50% to the composer and 50% to the publisher. But what Steve Swallow told me is that they went around and they talked to the Berklee guys who got their tunes in, from

Michael Gibbs to Pat Metheny, Swallow himself, Carla Bley, and so forth, who have these tunes in The Real Book, and he said the upshot of this was that these tunes, many of whom became part of the repertory, they were recorded over and over again and the recording royalties that they earned swamped, were hugely more, than anything that they ever would have collectively made from print versions had those tunes been published as sheet music.
That’s positive. Didn’t they call that the “butterfly effect?”
